title: Data Manipulation with R
subtitle: Sorting, filtering, grouping, transforming and combining datasets.
description: Develop practical data manipulation skills for extracting useful information from large datasets.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Understand Data Manipulation with R

Welcome to Lesson 7: Data Manipulation with R. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Data Manipulation with R”. The goal is to sorting, filtering, grouping, transforming and combining datasets.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Data manipulation transforms a dataset into the shape needed for analysis: filter relevant rows, select useful columns, create derived values, arrange records, and summarize groups.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 1: Data Manipulation with R in practice
blocks.code:
data <- data.frame(name = c("Ama", "Kojo", "Esi"), score = c(84, 67, 91))
subset(data, score >= 80)

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Sorting, filtering, grouping, transforming and combining datasets. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: A project repeats the same validation rule in four places and the rules now disagree. What should be done?
options: Centralize the rule in a reusable function and test it.
Add a fifth copy.
Remove the validation everywhere.
Make the rule depend on screen size.
blocks.explanation: A single tested rule avoids inconsistent copies and reduces maintenance cost.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A single tested rule avoids inconsistent copies and reduces maintenance cost.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A single tested rule avoids inconsistent copies and reduces maintenance cost.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Build the idea step by step

The dashboard frames the practical purpose this way: “Develop practical data manipulation skills for extracting useful information from large datasets.” Use the examples as small experiments, not as code to memorize. A strong result is one you can explain and then adapt to a slightly different requirement.

blocks.title: Sample 2: Data Manipulation with R in practice
blocks.code:
data <- data.frame(group = c("A", "A", "B"), score = c(5, 7, 9))
aggregate(score ~ group, data, mean)

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real R project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A project’s output looks correct but the code is difficult to maintain. What is the best next step?
options: Rename every variable randomly.
Add a second implementation without removing the first.
Ignore structure because the output is right.
Separate responsibilities, improve names, and add targeted tests.
blocks.explanation: Maintainability and tests make later changes safer, beyond simply matching one output.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Maintainability and tests make later changes safer, beyond simply matching one output.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Maintainability and tests make later changes safer, beyond simply matching one output.

blocks.text: Keep transformations reproducible by expressing them in code rather than editing a spreadsheet manually. Make one logical transformation at a time so it can be checked and reused.

blocks.question: An application relies on a service that may be unavailable. Which state should the UI or CLI handle?
options: Success only.
A clear loading/success/error or recovery state.
No output until it crashes.
A fabricated result.
blocks.explanation: Real applications must communicate expected failure states and avoid claiming work succeeded when it did not.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Real applications must communicate expected failure states and avoid claiming work succeeded when it did not.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Real applications must communicate expected failure states and avoid claiming work succeeded when it did not.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Compare before-and-after row counts and inspect a small sample of the output. Unexpected row duplication or removal may indicate a join or filtering mistake.

blocks.question: What makes a final coding project reproducible?
options: A screenshot of a successful run only.
A single unexplained binary.
Source, clear run instructions, and testable expected behavior.
A note saying “works on my phone.”
blocks.explanation: Source and repeatable instructions let another person verify the behavior independently.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Source and repeatable instructions let another person verify the behavior independently.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Source and repeatable instructions let another person verify the behavior independently.

blocks.question: A final application calculates correct totals for typical inputs. What else should be tested before release?
options: Only the title font.
Only the happy path.
Invalid, empty, boundary, and error cases as well as normal input.
Nothing, because the examples ran once.
blocks.explanation: Boundary and failure-path testing catches common defects that a happy-path run misses.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Boundary and failure-path testing catches common defects that a happy-path run misses.
